Continue Nxeon's game-catalog provisioning integrity sweep. Fresh agent, no prior context — read this fully, then the state files, before acting.

*** CRITICAL: you are a background sub-agent. You do NOT receive external/Monitor/custom-event notifications — if you end your turn "waiting" for one, you HALT and the sweep stalls silently. NEVER park waiting for an event. For a slow game install, poll it YOURSELF in a single bash command with a bounded loop (e.g. `for i in $(seq 1 40); do <check> && break; sleep 30; done`, cap ~20-30 min total). If an install is too slow, record its state in PROGRESS.md, TEAR IT DOWN, move on. Keep working continuously through the remaining families until you finish or hit a genuine blocker, THEN report. ***

*** CRITICAL: NEVER tear down a test VM while its provisioning/job is still RUNNING or QUEUED — check job status first (see teardown.sh, which now refuses this itself and will exit 1). Tearing down mid-job previously wedged the shared worker's serial loop and delayed a REAL CUSTOMER's backup ~41 minutes. Wait for the job to reach a terminal state (DONE/FAILED) before tearing down, or use FORCE_TEARDOWN=1 only if you've deliberately confirmed the worker itself needs restarting. ***

*** ONLY ONE SWEEP AGENT MAY RUN AT A TIME. Before provisioning, check `ssh root@178.63.94.114 'qm list'` for an existing `t-<family>-*` VM. If one exists that isn't yours, STOP — do not provision alongside it. If you find a leftover `t-*` VM at the very start (before you've provisioned anything) with a terminal-state job, it's abandoned from an interrupted run — clean it via teardown.sh before starting fresh. ***

WHAT NXEON IS: a VPS/game-server hosting platform, codebase at /opt/nxeon on this primary Proxmox host (OVH Singapore). You run ON the primary; test VMs provision onto node-2 (178.63.94.114) via the platform's worker + Proxmox API.

THE TASK per family: (1) provision for real on node-2, (2) poll until it's actually up, (3) verify the real join port is reachable from OUTSIDE the box, (4) — most important — change a real setting via the platform's own config-apply path and confirm it took effect live (only palworld/minecraft/rust/valheim have a real-apply impl; for others, confirm one doesn't exist and document the gap — do NOT build new apply implementations), (5) tear down completely with teardown.sh once the job is terminal.

READ FIRST: /tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/sweep/PROGRESS.md (full log — read the tail for the most recent entries), RESULTS.md, and the harness scripts there (sweep-one.sh, teardown.sh, provision.ts, wait.sh, verify.sh, info.ts, udpcheck.sh, teardown-db.ts, status.ts) — read each before use. Also docs/DOCUMENTATION.md for write-up style, and `git log --oneline -15` in /opt/nxeon for the latest shipped fixes.

JUST COMPLETED (do NOT redo): rounds 1-4 covered ark, bedrock, conan, factorio, projectzomboid, satisfactory, terraria, tf2, vrising, unturned, tf2/squad/mordhau (bind-mount fix), eco, gmod, l4d2, plus the original 10-family round-1 set. REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES=["palworld","minecraft","rust","valheim"]. Known owner-decision items (skip, don't re-litigate): CS2 unsellable, Conan server binary won't start, Stationeers unsellable (image issue), DST unsellable (needs per-customer Klei token), tf2's entry-tier disk too small, catalog-wide disk-size audit.

REMAINING to sweep (skip any PROGRESS.md marks done): sdtd, enshrouded, theforest, sonsoftheforest, dragonwilds, sunkenland, abioticfactor, icarus, arkasa, soulmask, vintagestory, nightingale, spaceengineers, kf2, barotrauma, sandstorm, theisle, empyrion. Per prior static risk assessment: watch sdtd/nightingale/theisle for TCP-vs-UDP join-port mismatches (same class as tf2/unturned/gmod/eco — verify empirically, don't assume); watch abioticfactor/icarus/arkasa/soulmask/empyrion/spaceengineers/sandstorm/barotrauma for root-owned-mount-vs-non-root-uid (same class as tf2/conan/unturned/l4d2 — verify each independently).

HARD RULES:
- Never fabricate — every claim needs real evidence (off-box connection, RCON/log read-back, git log).
- Fix real bugs with minimal tested commits (tsc clean, tests at baseline — current known baseline is 1324 pass / 39 fail, of which 5 are a stale test-port artifact unrelated to your work and the rest are pre-existing/false-positive; if your own change adds a NEW failure investigate it, don't just note the count), deploy staging→prod per PROGRESS.md, document in docs/DOCUMENTATION.md.
- Tear down EVERY test VM before the next family (once its job is terminal — see above), always via teardown.sh (it also purges vzdump backup archives). Never leave two test VMs running.
- Before finishing/pausing, verify node-2 clean: no leaked test VMs (`ssh root@178.63.94.114 'qm list'`), no orphaned Server/PortForward/Job rows, /tank/backup/dump/ holds only real-VM archives (leave sausaugepro vmid-101 — a real customer backup).
- Never touch a real customer server, never send a ticket reply, never rotate a live credential. Owner/pricing/business calls → document as "needs owner decision" and move on.

CONCURRENCY: a security-hardening effort runs in parallel, editing /opt/nxeon/lib, /opt/nxeon/scripts, and docs/SECURITY.md. Stay in your lane (worker/game-config.ts, prisma/catalog.ts + seed files, lib/games.ts join-port overrides, docs/DOCUMENTATION.md); re-read a shared file right before editing it. Never run two prod builds at once. If provisioning suddenly fails with Proxmox AUTH errors, the token may have been rotated — STOP and report, don't retry in a loop.

REPORT when the remaining families are swept (or at a real blocker): what you did, bugs fixed w/ commit hashes, owner-decision items, families still unswept, and explicit confirmation node-2 is clean (no leaked VMs/rows/backups).

Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.

content.content:
Baseline at start: node-2 clean (no `t-*` VMs), no orphan Server/Job/PortForward rows,
`/tank/backup/dump/` holding only the real customer archive for vmid 101 (sausaugepro).

## Shipped this pass

| commit | what |
|---|---|
| `dc6e07f` | **Eco**: server never started (no `-offline`), and its join port was TCP for a UDP game |
| `b6cf476` | **Garry's Mod**: installed nothing (`GAME_ID=template`), and Source families forwarded RCON instead of the game |
| `b97d143` | **Left 4 Dead 2**: both bind mounts unwritable by the container |

## Global finding: only 5 families have ANY real-apply path

`worker/game-config.ts`'s `applyRealConfig` switch has exactly five cases —
`minecraft`, `rust`, `valheim`, `cs2`, `palworld`. **Every other family falls to the
default (simulated) case.** So sweep step (4) "change a real setting and confirm it
took effect" is not applicable to any family in this pass: the gap is uniform and
structural, not per-family. `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` remains
`["palworld","minecraft","rust","valheim"]` (cs2 has an impl but cannot provision).

## Per-family log

| family | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| necesse | **verified-full** | job=DONE 350s. World generated, "Started server using port 14159 with 10 slots". External UDP proven end-to-end (node DNAT 14->20, in-guest tcpdump `docker0 Out > 172.17.0.2.14159`) — and the game itself logged the probe ("Server received unknown packet from client N/A"). Container runs as root; data in the mount. No real-apply. |
| eco | **verified-full + 2 REAL BUGS FIXED** (`dc6e07f`) | see below |
| stationeers | **FAILED — needs owner decision** | see below |
| gmod | **verified-full + 2 REAL BUGS FIXED** (`b6cf476`) | see below |
| l4d2 | **verified-connectivity + REAL BUG FIXED** (`b97d143`) | job=DONE 295s. Forward corrected to 27015/udp->20021, UDP proven end-to-end. Both bind mounts were unwritable by uid 1000 — fixed + re-verified live. |
| corekeeper | **verified-full** | job=DONE 264s. World created (11 content bundles, world version Ck121), session started with a real Core Keeper join ID. 653M in the mount, container root. External UDP proven (DNAT 5->11 + in-guest tcpdump). No real-apply. |
| dst | **FAILED — needs owner decision** | see below |
| mordhau | **already verified in `0eadce7`** — not re-run | that commit verified it live end-to-end (job=DONE, mount owned 1000 with 5.2GB in it, 7777/udp reachable). |

### Eco — was 100% unprovisionable, two independent faults (FIXED, shipped `dc6e07f`)

1. **EcoServer never started.** `emackie/steamcmd-eco`'s entrypoint execs `EcoServer`
   with no arguments and offers no hook to add any, and EcoServer exits 232:
   "Authentication to Strange Cloud failed. No authentication methods were available…
   or use '-offline'". Under the provisioning wrapper's systemd unit that is a crash
   loop — caught live at `NRestarts=30` with no listener ever opening.
2. **`GAME_PORT.eco` said 3000/tcp; Eco's game port is UDP.** Read off a running
   EcoServer's own `/proc/net`: `udp:3000` bound, `tcp:3001` (WebServer), `tcp:3002`
   (RCON), and **no `tcp:3000` at all**. The setup script published only
   `-p 3000:3000/tcp`. Checked whether this fails loudly or silently: docker-proxy
   *refuses* the connect rather than accepting it ("connect to 10.20.1.106 port 3000
   (tcp) failed: Connection refused"), so it was a hard failure — but the forward
   handed to a customer would also have been TCP for a UDP-only game.

After the fix, fresh provision: **job=DONE in 444s**, "Server Initialization … Finished",
world saved (692 storages persisted), forward `3000/udp->20015`, external UDP proven
end-to-end (DNAT 10->16 + in-guest tcpdump). 522M in the mount, container runs as root.

**Owner decision:** `-offline` means direct-connect only — the server is not listed in
Eco's public browser. Listing one requires the customer's own paid Eco account
(`-userToken` / `-username`). Collecting that in the panel is a product call.

### Garry's Mod — was 100% unprovisionable + a cross-family port bug (FIXED, shipped `b6cf476`)

1. **Nothing ever installed.** `ghcr.io/ich777/steamcmd:garrysmod` is ich777's
   **template** image: `GAME_ID=template`, `GAME_NAME=template`, `GAME_PARAMS=template`
   read straight off the image. The appid is supplied per container. The setupScript
   overrode only `GAME_PARAMS`, so the entrypoint ran `+app_update template validate` —
   a silent no-op (SteamCMD connects, downloads nothing, exits 0) — `srcds_run` never
   existed, and start-server.sh died on "No such file or directory". Permanent crash
   loop, caught at **`NRestarts=61` with 8.0K in a perfectly writable bind mount**.
   The wave7 seed comment claimed the binary "is pulled fresh via `+app_update 4020`
   at every container start". That was an assumption and it was never true.
   With `GAME_ID=4020` the same container downloaded **6,870,007,094 bytes (6.4 GiB)**.
2. **Source-engine families were forwarded on the wrong protocol.** srcds binds the
   same port NUMBER on both protocols and they are different services: **UDP 27015 is
   the game + A2S query protocol, TCP 27015 is RCON.** Proven on the running server —
   an A2S_INFO datagram to UDP 27015 answered `ff ff ff ff 41 …` (S2C_CHALLENGE) while
   TCP 27015 accepted the connection and returned **nothing** to the same query.
   `joinPortFor` had no entry, so provisioning forwarded 27015/**tcp**.

   Because the port numbers match, this hid where rust/ark/factorio did not: the
   dashboard address looked right while players could not connect, and the single port
   left published to the internet was **RCON** — the exact exposure `196e5c9` closed.
   `gmod/tf2/l4d2/cs2` now override to 27015/udp; `GAME_PORT` stays TCP as the honest
   liveness check. +1 test.

After the fix, fresh provision: **job=DONE in 454s**, 6.5G in the mount, srcds up,
forward `27015/udp->20018`, and — the strongest evidence available — a real
**A2S_INFO query sent from OFF-BOX to `178.63.94.114:20018` got a Source
`S2C_CHALLENGE` reply**, which is exactly what a player's server browser does.

l4d2 independently confirmed the same shape (binds both tcp:27015 and udp:27015).
**tf2 remains unconfirmed against a real server** — same srcds binary and same
mapping, but it is still on the unswept list.

### Stationeers — installs fine, game never starts (owner decision)

Installs cleanly (13.3 GB into a writable mount, container healthy, no restart loop)
but the game **never binds any port, TCP or UDP**, and never creates a world —
`saves/` stayed empty after 10+ minutes across three separate configurations.

Root cause: `didstopia/stationeers-server` drives the current Stationeers build with
stale CLI flags, and hardcodes them so they cannot be overridden. Its `start.sh`
always appends `-worldname=X -loadworld=X`, unquoted, from image ENV defaults
(`STATIONEERS_WORLD_NAME=docker`, `STATIONEERS_SERVER_NAME=A Docker Server`) — and
because it tests with `${VAR+x}` (set-or-not), passing an empty value does not
suppress them. Three findings, in order of discovery:

1. The catalog sets `STATIONEERS_WORLD_NAME='Nxeon World'` — a value **with a space**,
   which the image interpolates unquoted, so argv split into `-worldname=Nxeon`,
   `World`, `-loadworld=Nxeon`, `World`. Genuinely broken, but not the whole story.
2. With a valid single-token world type (`moon`) the args were correct and it still
   never bound a port or wrote a save in 10 minutes.
3. Passing modern `-settings StartLocalHost true …` via
   `STATIONEERS_SERVER_STARTUP_ARGUMENTS` still had the image's baked-in legacy flags
   appended after it; the container exited 127.

**Needs the owner:** this is an image-replacement decision (or a full entrypoint
override, as was done for Eco), not a setup-script tweak. Not guessed at here.
Stationeers is not sellable today.

### Don't Starve Together — 100% unsellable, needs a per-customer token (owner decision)

The server refuses to start, in its own words:

```
[200] Account Failed (6): "E_INVALID_TOKEN"
!!!! Your Server Will Not Start !!!!
No auth token could be found.
Please visit https://accounts.klei.com/account/game/servers?game=DontStarveTogether
```

The setup script passes `-e TOKEN=''`. DST requires a **Klei cluster token**, which is
generated from the *customer's own Klei account* — there is no anonymous or
platform-wide equivalent, so this is not fixable in the setup script.

Note this contradicts the standing catalog rationale. `seed-wave9-games.ts` groups
"DST's TOKEN" with Dragonwilds' OWNER_ID as customer-specific values where "the
container boots and is reachable with sane defaults out of the box, and the customer
edits the mounted config file post-deploy via SFTP". For DST that is **factually
false**: it does not boot at all. Selling DST needs the panel to collect a Klei
cluster token at order time (or immediately post-deploy, with the server held).

### Other findings

- **Core Keeper joins by Game ID, not IP:port, and advertises the wrong port.** Its
  session line reads `178.63.94.114;27015;<id>;<key>` — the **guest-side** port. NAT
  maps public `20018 -> guest 27015`, so a player using the advertised Game ID would
  be sent to `178.63.94.114:27015`, which is not forwarded. Worth an owner/architecture
  look for any family that advertises its own port to a lobby/relay rather than being
  handed one. Not changed here.
- **L4D2 disk is tight**: 20G used of a 24G root fs (84%) on the entry plan. Fits, but
  it is the closest call seen so far outside the known CS2/TF2 cases.
- **L4D2 does not answer A2S even from inside the guest** while hibernating, alongside
  `[S_API FAIL] SteamAPI_Init() failed`. The port is bound and reachable (proven), so
  this is reported as an observation, not a proven defect — but no family currently
  passes a Steam Game Server Login Token, which is what public server-browser listing
  needs. Owner call.
- **Test baseline moved 34 -> 39 failures** during this pass, from the concurrent
  security-hardening lane (node-agent, rate-limit-IP, "use server" auth tests), not
  from this sweep. My own changes kept `test/provision-health.test.ts` green (24/24)
  and tsc clean.

### Process lesson — do not tear down under a live job

Tearing down stationeers while the worker still had a provisioning ATTEMPT in flight
wedged the worker's single job loop against a VM that no longer existed: it kept
probing a destroyed guest, and because the loop is serial **a real customer's
BACKUP_CREATE job sat QUEUED behind it for ~40 minutes**. Cleared by restarting
`nxeon-worker` (by unit, per the standing rule — never by pattern); the customer's
backup then ran and completed immediately. `teardown.sh` now refuses to run while the

Continuing through the other game servers, I'm noting similar potential permission mismatches for enshrouded, theforest, abioticfactor, icarus, arkasa, and soulmask where directories get created without explicit chown, though some LGSM-style images handle chowning internally at startup. I confirm the disk-sizing fix uses the max of the two plan values, which checks out.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Sweep several families back to back. Tears a family down ONLY if its PROVISION
# job reached DONE and the external reachability check passed; otherwise it stops
# the whole batch and leaves the VM up for review. Appends one result line per
# family to RESULTS.md.
# Usage: batch.sh <family> [family...]
set -u
SW=/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/sweep
RES="$SW/RESULTS.md"

for FAM in "$@"; do
  echo "=================== $FAM ==================="
  OUT=$(bash "$SW/sweep-one.sh" "$FAM" 2700 2>&1)
  printf '%s\n' "$OUT"
  printf '%s\n' "$OUT" > "$SW/out-$FAM.txt"

  SID=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | sed -n 's/^### END .* (serverId=\([^ ]*\) vmid=\([0-9]*\))$/\1/p' | tail -1)
  VMID=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | sed -n 's/^### END .* (serverId=\([^ ]*\) vmid=\([0-9]*\))$/\2/p' | tail -1)

  if printf '%s' "$OUT" | grep -q "SKIP — "; then
    echo "| $FAM | no-gameplan | skipped, no GamePlan row |" >> "$RES"
    continue
  fi

  DONE=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | grep -c '"status":"DONE"')
  REACH=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | grep -cE "succeeded!|packets captured")
  if [ "$DONE" -ge 1 ] && [ "$REACH" -ge 1 ]; then
    echo "| $FAM | verified-provisioning+connectivity | job DONE, external reachability proven |" >> "$RES"
    bash "$SW/teardown.sh" "$SID" "$VMID" 2>&1 | tail -2
  else
    echo "!!! $FAM did NOT cleanly verify (DONE=$DONE REACH=$REACH) — leaving VM $VMID up for review, stopping batch"
    echo "| $FAM | NEEDS REVIEW | job DONE=$DONE reachable=$REACH — serverId=$SID vmid=$VMID |" >> "$RES"
    exit 1
  fi
done
echo "=================== BATCH COMPLETE ==================="

content.thinking:
Confirmed the config only has queryPort: 15637 with no gamePort key at all — Enshrouded's dedicated server moved to a single UDP port after a mid-2024 update, replacing the old two-port scheme of 15636 game + 15637 query.

So the assumption that game port 15636/udp exists is wrong — nothing ever binds to it. The forwarded 15636/udp mapping is useless since players can't connect there, and if the health check probes 15636/udp it should never pass, meaning any Enshrouded order should hang and eventually fail. I need to check how the UDP probe behaves on silence — since docker-proxy is listening on 15636 but forwarding to a container with nothing there, the container's ICMP unreachable response goes back to docker-proxy rather than the prober, so the probe likely just sees silence. Empirically the job is still running at 30 minutes with the "installing the game" step, which is a large download.

The check must be failing on silence, confirming this is a genuine, reproducible bug: Enshrouded is currently unsellable since every order fails the game-port check, and even if it somehow passed, the forwarded port would be dead anyway. The fix should be updating GAME_PORT.enshrouded to point at 15637/udp instead of 15636. I want to double check that Enshrouded really only uses a single port now by looking at whether the image's config file has a gamePort key and confirming the running server only binds 15637, then grep the logs for "port" to be sure, and verify players' clients can actually query the server via Steam A2S on 15637.

Now I want to verify that Enshrouded's connect UI really does use the query port (15637) as the "IP:Port" players enter, and check how long the job's extended wait runs before failing so I know when it becomes safe to tear down.

content.content:
#!/bin/bash
# Deploy a ref (default: main from /opt/nxeon) to the staging environment.
# Usage: ./scripts/deploy-staging.sh [git-ref]
set -euo pipefail
REF="${1:-main}"
cd /opt/nxeon-staging

echo "==> Syncing staging to $REF"
git fetch origin
git reset --hard "origin/$REF"

echo "==> Installing dependencies"
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -1

echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss 2>&1 | tail -2
npm run db:seed 2>&1 | tail -2 || true

echo "==> Building"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4

# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. Only .next needs to be writable by
# it (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable, and systemd
# injects .env as root. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon-staging/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon-staging/.env 2>/dev/null || true

echo "==> Restarting staging services"
systemctl restart nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
echo "==> Staging responds: HTTP $CODE (http://$(grep ^PUBLIC_IP .env | cut -d= -f2):8080)"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "STAGING UNHEALTHY"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Staging deploy complete"
=== PROMOTE ===
#!/bin/bash
# Promote the currently deployed staging commit to production.
# Verifies staging is healthy, fast-forwards nothing (prod working tree IS the repo),
# then rebuilds + restarts production services.
set -euo pipefail

STG_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon-staging rev-parse HEAD)
PROD_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon rev-parse HEAD)

echo "==> Staging is at:    $STG_COMMIT"
echo "==> Production is at: $PROD_COMMIT"

if ! systemctl is-active -q nxeon-staging-web; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging web service is not running." >&2
  exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
if [ "$CODE" != "200" ]; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging returns HTTP $CODE." >&2
  exit 1
fi

if [ "$STG_COMMIT" != "$PROD_COMMIT" ]; then
  echo "Note: production tree is at a different commit than staging."
  echo "Production deploys directly from /opt/nxeon's working tree (main)."
fi

cd /opt/nxeon
echo "==> Installing dependencies (adds any new deps before build)"
# CRITICAL: without this, a commit that adds a new dependency (e.g. imapflow)
# builds against a stale node_modules and fails — which previously aborted the
# promote AFTER the old build was already gone. Always sync deps first.
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -3
# CRITICAL: this was previously `prisma generate` only — regenerates the
# CLIENT's types (fixes the build) but never touches the actual DATABASE.
# Staging and production are SEPARATE databases (nxeon_staging vs nxeon, same
# Postgres server, confirmed live) — deploy-staging.sh's own `db push` only
# ever applies to staging's DB, so a schema change promoted this way built
# and deployed fine while production's actual table never got the new
# column, silently breaking the FIRST thing that queried it post-deploy
# (found live 2026-09-02: worker/billing.ts's sweeps started throwing
# "column does not exist" immediately after a routine promote — no staging
# failure gave any warning, since staging's own db push had already
# succeeded there). `db push` both applies the schema AND regenerates the
# client, so this replaces the old generate-only step rather than adding a
# second one. Schema changes are rare enough that this always running
# unconditionally costs nothing when there's nothing new to push.
echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --schema=/opt/nxeon/prisma/schema.prisma 2>&1 | tail -4
echo "==> Building production"

 * WHY THIS EXISTS: the whole game control panel — GAME_POWER start/stop/restart,
 * GAME_BACKUP, log tailing (lib/game-control.ts + worker/game-control.ts) —

 * so every one of those lookups comes back empty and every control action fails

 * started/stopped from the dashboard even though PROVISION had completed
 * successfully — the container was in fact running, just entirely invisible to
 * systemd.
 *
 * The generated unit is named after the family's FIRST serviceHint, not the
 * docker container's own `--name` — the two don't always match (minecraft's
 * image runs as container "mc" but its control-spec hints are "minecraft" /
 * "minecraft-server") — so `systemctl cat <hint>` resolves regardless of what an
 * individual image's setup script happened to call its container.
 *
 * Intentionally conservative: any setupScript that doesn't match the exact
 * `docker run -d --name X ...` shape (or any non-game family, e.g. the
 * LAMP/WordPress/Caddy panel images that already install a real native systemd
 * service) is returned completely unchanged.
 */
function wrapDockerGameService(setupScript: string, family: string | null): string {
  if (!isGameFamily(family)) return setupScript;
  const unitName = controlSpec(family)?.serviceHints[0];
  if (!unitName) return setupScript;

  const re = /docker run\s+(?:-d|--detach)\b(.*?)\s+--name[= ]("?)([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\2(.*)$/.exec(setupScript.trim());
  if (!re) return setupScript;
  const [full, before, , containerName, after] = re;
  const matchIndex = setupScript.indexOf(full);
  if (matchIndex < 0) return setupScript;

  // Strip docker's own restart policy — systemd now owns restart semantics for
  // this container, and leaving both in place makes the two supervisors fight
  // over a crash-looping process.
  const cleanedAfter = after.replace(/\s*--restart(?:=|\s+)\S+/, "");
  const createCmd = `docker create --name ${containerName}${before}${cleanedAfter}`.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();

  const prefix = setupScript.slice(0, matchIndex);
  const unit = [
    `cat > /etc/systemd/system/${unitName}.service <<'NXUNIT'`,
    "[Unit]",
    `Description=Nxeon game service (docker: ${containerName})`,
    "After=docker.service",
    "Requires=docker.service",
    "",
    "[Service]",
    `ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker start -a ${containerName}`,
    `ExecStop=/usr/bin/docker stop -t 30 ${containerName}`,
    "Restart=always",
    "RestartSec=5",
    "TimeoutStartSec=0",
    "",
    "[Install]",
    "WantedBy=multi-user.target",
    "NXUNIT",
    "systemctl daemon-reload",
    `systemctl enable --now ${unitName}`,
  ].join("\n");

  return `${prefix}${createCmd}\n${unit}`;
}

input.new_string:
/** Consecutive no-progress samples before giving up. */
export const GAME_INSTALL_STALL_LIMIT = 3;
/**
 * Restarts of the game's own systemd unit, accumulated DURING the extended
 * wait, that mean "crash loop" rather than "still installing".
 *
 * Why: `installProgressed` treats any container output inside the sample
 * window as work in progress — and a container that dies and is restarted by
 * systemd every few seconds produces output continuously, forever. So a
 * genuinely broken family never trips the stall detector and burns the entire
 * `GAME_INSTALL_MAX_WAIT_MS` ceiling on every one of its three attempts.
 * Measured on the families this catalog sweep found broken: Eco (caught at
 * NRestarts=30), Garry's Mod (61), The Forest (19 within nine minutes) — each
 * one made a customer watch "Installing the game…" for ~2.25 hours before
 * being told it failed, when the guest knew inside a minute.
 *
 * The generated unit (`wrapDockerGameService`) is `Restart=always`
 * `RestartSec=5`, and a healthy install never exits at all, so NRestarts stays
 * 0 for every family that works. Counting the DELTA since the wait began — not
 * the absolute value — keeps a container that legitimately restarted once or
 * twice during earlier setup from being judged on that history.
 */
export const GAME_INSTALL_RESTART_LIMIT = 3;

/**
 * Has the game's systemd unit restarted enough times DURING the extended wait
 * to call it a crash loop? A negative reading means "unknown" (no unit, or the
 * guest could not be asked) and is never treated as a crash — this check can
 * only ever end a wait early on positive evidence.
 */
export function gameUnitCrashLooping(firstRestarts: number, currentRestarts: number): boolean {
  if (!Number.isFinite(firstRestarts) || !Number.isFinite(currentRestarts)) return false;
  if (firstRestarts < 0 || currentRestarts < 0) return false;
  return currentRestarts - firstRestarts >= GAME_INSTALL_RESTART_LIMIT;
}

content.thinking:
I've found something big: udpAttempt actually resolves to success on timeout rather than failure, meaning the UDP game-port check always reports true for any reachable host regardless of whether anything's actually listening — it's a fake check that proves nothing. Right now theforest is crash-looping with 114 restarts, nothing's listening on any UDP port in the guest since docker-proxy disappears when the container exits, yet the provisioning job still reports success.

The reason attempt 1 failed but attempt 2 passed makes sense now — when the container is down, the guest returns ICMP port-unreachable, which surfaces as ECONNREFUSED and fails the check; when the container happens to be up (even briefly during its restart cycle), there's no ICMP response so the check times out and falsely reports success. So attempt 2 just got lucky by sampling during one of the container's brief "up" windows.

This exposes a serious systemic bug: the UDP health check treats a timeout as success, meaning it verifies nothing — a crash-looping container can report DONE without any game actually running, since the check only needs one lucky sample across 300 seconds of retries.

The proper fix should verify the port is actually bound inside the guest via SSH, since that's protocol-independent and decisive, rather than relying on the external UDP probe which can't distinguish "nothing rejected" from "something is listening." For UDP, I'm thinking the check needs both an external probe showing the packet wasn't refused and internal confirmation the game process actually bound the port.

I think it's cleaner to keep the combination logic inside provision-health.ts so it stays unit-testable, rather than splitting the UDP bind confirmation into worker/index.ts. I'm sketching a helper that checks whether a given UDP port is actually bound inside the guest, designed to be testable with an injectable probe.

But then I realize a snag: the port gets bound by docker-proxy in the guest's root network namespace, not by the game process itself, so docker-proxy will show the port as bound as soon as the container is running even if the game inside never actually binds anything -- which undermines using /proc/net/udp as a reliable signal.

The real fix is to look inside the container's own network namespace instead, the way ctports.sh does, since that's what actually proves the game bound the port rather than just proving the container is up. I'm sketching a guest-side shell loop that finds running container PIDs, checks each one's /proc/<pid>/net/udp and udp6 for the target port using awk, and reports back whether it found the port bound.

I should also cover the guest root netns for host-network containers or native installs. This is a bigger change, but it's arguably the single highest-value fix available since it stops the platform from shipping dead UDP servers as "ready" — though I need to weigh the risk that it could introduce false negatives and break provisioning for working orders across every UDP family, especially for games that bind lazily after the first packet rather than at startup.

Looking back at the families verified this sweep — palworld, valheim, ark, eco, gmod, l4d2, corekeeper, necesse, unturned, mordhau — all had genuinely bound ports proven via ctports/tcpdump, so they'd pass under a stricter check. I think the safe design is: UDP passes only when the external probe isn't refused AND the port is actually bound in some netns on the guest, requiring positive evidence rather than just absence of a refusal. I'll need to thread an optional async bind-verification callback into checkGamePortOpen so it's used both in the initial check and in the extended wait loop, which altogether feels like a 30-45 minute task including tests.

This is worth fixing rather than just reporting, since it's a real bug with a minimal, testable fix, and it directly undermines trust in the rest of the sweep results — the timeout path currently resolves as ok:true, and the function's own claim that it verifies the game process bound the port is false for UDP. I want to empirically confirm this false-positive right now before proceeding.

I have concrete evidence: the live theforest guest has nothing listening on 27015/udp, yet the job reports DONE, so I'll run the actual udpAttempt logic against the real forward to demonstrate it incorrectly returns ok.

This is interesting — the UDP check returned false with ECONNREFUSED this time, because the container was down at the sampling moment, triggering an ICMP unreachable. When the container briefly comes up, docker-proxy binds the port and there's no ICMP response, so the check times out and reports true instead. So this health check is essentially a coin flip against a crash-looping container depending on timing.

But wait, this contradicts what I saw with enshrouded — docker-proxy was listening on the guest port for 45+ minutes while the game bound nothing, yet the check stayed failing rather than flipping to true. The difference must be that enshrouded's check target was going through a NAT forward from public port to guest port, not hitting the guest port directly, so I need to reconsider how the routing path affects whether docker-proxy's response actually reaches the checker.

That explains why enshrouded fails - the worker sees ECONNREFUSED once the ICMP unreachable propagates back through the DNAT chain. This means theforest would return ok:true only during a narrow race window: while the container is starting or stopping, packets get silently dropped (no ICMP, no route) rather than refused, and a dropped packet reads as a timeout, which the check treats as success.

With 118 restarts and roughly 60 check attempts over 300 seconds, there are more than enough such windows to guarantee a false pass. So the bug is real and defensible: the check treats absence of evidence as proof of success, backed by both the code's timeout-as-success logic and the live outcome — job marked DONE while the server's own log says it aborted startup. The fix needs to require positive proof the game actually bound its port rather than just an absence of rejection.

I'm designing a helper that parses /proc/net/udp or /proc/net/tcp tables to detect whether a given port is bound or listening, then a worker-side function that SSHes into the guest to verify the bind directly. The plan is to combine the external port probe with this in-guest bind check for UDP so a positive result requires both signals to agree.

If the bind check comes back false, I'll treat the overall reachability check as failed, letting it fall into the install-wait logic which handles crash loops and genuine installs -- applying the same combined logic during the per-sample rechecks there too. Writing the wrapper function now...

Writing the check logic...

But wait, I'm worried about the cost—for a UDP probe that just times out silently, this would trigger an SSH bind check every 5 seconds for 300 seconds, meaning 60 separate SSH connections, which feels excessive and risky under load. A better approach might be to run the network retry loop on its own first, and only fire a single bind verification once it actually succeeds, retrying that verification separately if needed.

Actually, a simpler design occurs to me: for UDP families, treat the in-guest bind check as the real signal, with the external probe just as a lightweight secondary confirmation—so I'd run the cheap probe, and only if it doesn't outright refuse would I fall back to a bind check on a slower cadence, like every 15 seconds instead of every 5. Since SSH connects are roughly 200ms and the worker runs serially anyway, even 60 connections over five minutes during provisioning is probably tolerable in practice.

But I realize checkGamePortOpen samples over a 60-second window, which means 12 reads per minute compounding over a 45-minute wait — that's far too many SSH connections. So I want to only trigger the bind verification on a successful probe, but for UDP the probe basically always "succeeds" since silence means success, so it'd fire every single attempt anyway. That pushes me toward just replacing the UDP probe outright with the in-guest bind check as the primary signal, running at a slower cadence instead of every attempt.

That gives one SSH read per attempt at a 10-second interval, which nets out to roughly 30 reads over 300 seconds, or about 6 reads per minute within each 60-second window. I'm weighing whether to drop the external UDP probe entirely since it adds no real signal when silence equals success, but that loses the "NAT path actually works" verification, whereas TCP families still get the true external check. Given the goal of testing things the way a real customer would, I'm leaning toward requiring both signals for UDP, but evaluating the cheap network probe first and only falling back to the SSH bind read second.

Stop marking a dead UDP game server as ready

`udpAttempt` resolves SUCCESS on timeout. For a connectionless protocol a
generic prober has nothing else to go on — a healthy game server owes no reply
to a byte of nonsense — so the UDP half of the game-port check passed on
silence, and silence is exactly what a guest emits while a crash-looping
container sits between restarts: the packet is dropped rather than refused.
Most of this catalog joins on UDP, so most of the catalog was not being checked
at all.

Caught live on node-2 rather than reasoned about: a The Forest order reached
PROVISION DONE and would have been handed to a customer as ready while its
container had restarted 118 times, had never started the game
("Missing SERVER_STEAM_ACCOUNT_TOKEN … Aborting server start"), and had nothing
bound to any port in its namespace. That is the same "the system asserting
something untrue" failure this module was written to end, on the protocol half
nobody had checked.

The check now also demands positive evidence from inside the guest: the port
must appear in a `/proc/net` table. Which namespace is the whole point —
`docker-proxy` binds every published port in the guest's ROOT namespace for as
long as the container is up, whether or not the game inside ever listens (The
Forest's guest showed `0.0.0.0:27015` bound with the game dead), so running
containers' namespaces are read and the root one is used only when no container
is running. A `--network host` container is unaffected: its namespace is the
root one.

Fails open by construction. An unreadable guest returns null, never false, so
an SSH hiccup can never turn a healthy server into a failed order; only an
actual absent binding does. Applied to the extended install wait too, so that
path cannot end on silence either.

+6 tests, over real `/proc/net` table text captured from a guest.

The current server is **single-port**: the image's own generated `enshrouded_server.json`
carries a `queryPort` key and **no `gamePort` key at all**, the process had udp:15637 bound
and nothing on 15636, and A2S_INFO to 15637 answered S2C_CHALLENGE while 15636 was silent.

So the health check probed a port nothing binds. The server was fully healthy the whole time
(world generated, saving, "Snapshot took 575us … Entities: 1,829") while the order sat in
"Installing the game…". Worse, `waitOutGameInstall` reads the container's 30-second heartbeat
as progress, so the stall detector never tripped: **45 min per attempt × 3 = ~2.25 hours**
before failing. And had it passed, the single forward handed to the customer was the dead port.

Verified after the fix on the SAME running VM (idempotent retry, nothing reinstalled):
job **DONE in 3 min**, forward `15637/udp->20018`, and an **A2S_INFO sent from off-box to
`178.63.94.114:20018` answered `ffffffff416c4b3fff`** — exactly what a player's client gets.
The old forward (`15636 -> 20015`), i.e. what every customer got, stayed **silent**.
No real-apply (default case).

### theforest — FAILED, needs owner decision (Steam GSLT)
Installs fine (1.7G, mount `1000:1000` and writable — mount class clear). The game never
starts: the image aborts before launch —

```
> Checking for existence of SERVER_STEAM_ACCOUNT_TOKEN
>>> Missing SERVER_STEAM_ACCOUNT_TOKEN detected: Please add a token. Aborting server start ...
```

Confirmed in the image itself (`/includes/security.sh` `check_for_default_credentials`:
`[[ -z $SERVER_STEAM_ACCOUNT_TOKEN ]] && exit 1`), and `/includes/config.sh` maps it to the
game's own `serverSteamAccount` setting. That is a **Steam Game Server Login Token**, minted
per Steam account + AppID. The setup script passes none, so the unit crash-loops forever
(caught at NRestarts=118).

**Needs the owner** — same shape as DST's Klei token: either collect a GSLT at order time, or
issue Nxeon-owned GSLTs (one Steam account, and a ban on it propagates to every server on it).
Contradicts the wave-seed rationale that these containers "boot with sane defaults and the
customer edits config post-deploy" — this one does not boot at all.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

# Check if .X1-lock file exists and remove. Otherwise Xvfb cannot start.
[ -f /tmp/.X1-lock ] && rm -f /tmp/.X1-lock

_terminate() {
  echo "Caught TERM signal!"
  echo "Stopping Sunkenland"
  wineserver -k -w
  /etc/init.d/xvfb stop
}

trap _terminate HUP INT QUIT TERM

if [ -z "${GAME_WORLD_GUID}" ]; then
  echo "Please set environment variable 'GAME_WORLD_GUID', game cannot start otherwise."
  exit 1
fi

if [ -z "${GAME_REGION}" ]; then
  GAME_REGION=eu
fi

if [[ ${GAME_MAX_PLAYER} =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
  MAX_PLAYER_PARAM=" -maxPlayerCapacity ${GAME_MAX_PLAYER}"
fi

if [ "${GAME_SESSION_INVISIBLE}" = true ]; then
  SESSION_INVISIBLE=" -makeSessionInvisible true"
fi

if [ "$GAME_UPDATE" = true ] || [ -z "$(ls -A /sunkenland/game)" ]; then
  if [ -n "${GAME_BETA_VERSION}" ]; then
    BETA_VERSION=" -beta ${GAME_BETA_VERSION}"
    echo "Updating to beta version ${GAME_BETA_VERSION}"
  fi
  echo "Start game update..."
  steamcmd +force_install_dir /${USER_NAME}/game +@sSteamCmdForcePlatformType windows +login anonymous +app_update \
           "${APP_ID}" ${BETA_VERSION} validate +quit
  echo "Game update done"
fi

/etc/init.d/xvfb start
wine /${USER_NAME}/game/Sunkenland-DedicatedServer.exe -nographics -batchmode -worldGuid ${GAME_WORLD_GUID}${MAX_PLAYER_PARAM}${SESSION_INVISIBLE} -password "${GAME_PASSWORD}" -region "${GAME_REGION}" &

wait

content.thinking:
I'm looking at the launch command for the dedicated server, which runs the executable via wine with flags for headless mode, world GUID, player limits, session visibility, password, and region — noting the catalog hardcodes the world GUID to 'nxeon-world'.

The "Invalid Server Config" error likely stems from `-worldGuid` needing an actual generated GUID tied to an existing world save, not an arbitrary string like "nxeon-world" — Sunkenland's docs indicate the GUID comes from the world folder name created by the client. I also notice no `-port` argument is passed anywhere in the script, even though the container exposes 27015/27016 UDP, which could be another source of the misconfiguration.

I want to test this empirically by trying a properly formatted GUID to see if the error persists, which would tell me whether the issue is GUID format versus the world needing to pre-exist. There's also a bigger concern: the WORLD_FOLDER path points into the Wine AppData directory rather than the mounted `/sunkenland/Worlds` volume, which could mean customer world data isn't actually being persisted outside the container — a separate potential bug worth checking by inspecting the running container's filesystem.

Close two ways the UDP bind check could still pass a dead server

reached PROVISION DONE with its game dead on "Invalid Server Config", nothing
bound to any port in the container's namespace, and the container up (so the
crash-loop detector had nothing to see either). Two holes, both of them the
check quietly deciding an absence of information was a pass.

1. UNKNOWN COUNTED AS OPEN. The in-guest read returns null when the guest
   cannot be asked, and null was treated as "fine, carry on". For TCP that is
   correct — the completed connect is evidence on its own. For UDP it is not:
   the probe reports success on silence, so with no in-guest answer the attempt
   established nothing, and any transient SSH hiccup restored the original
   no-op check. UDP now requires a positive answer. Attempts repeat across the
   whole retry window, so a blip costs one attempt; only a guest unreachable
   for the entire window fails, and that guest has a real problem anyway.

2. A FAILED `docker ps` LOOKED LIKE "NO CONTAINERS". Its output is empty in
   both cases, and empty meant "fall back to the guest's root namespace" —
   exactly where docker-proxy answers for a game that never started. Its exit
   status is now captured, so an unqueryable daemon reads as UNKNOWN. The root
   namespace is used only when docker cleanly reports zero running containers,
   in which case docker-proxy is gone too and the reading is honest.

Both verdicts are also logged now, with the reason. A check that silently
decides is how this got through twice.

+2 tests on the verdict rule, which is now a named pure function rather than
inline branches.

content.thinking:
That log line is key—the game binds port 17777 through SteamNetDriver, meaning it's using Steam's relay networking rather than opening a genuine OS-level UDP socket. That explains why only port 27015 shows up in /proc/net/udp; 17777 is just a logical port used by Steam's relay, not something that can actually be port-forwarded.

This means the health check and forward for 17777/udp are fundamentally broken since nothing ever binds to it—Icarus is essentially unsellable as currently configured. The real fix likely means switching GAME_PORT.icarus to 27015/udp, the port the server actually binds, though this raises the same NAT/advertised-port mismatch problem seen with Core Keeper, since Steam's server list would broadcast the wrong public port after forwarding.

Fixing the check to point at the correct port is a genuine improvement since it stops failing for the wrong reason, but I need to verify joinability is actually provable rather than assumed. I should test whether 27015 answers the A2S query protocol from off-box or from the guest—if it responds, that confirms Steam's server browser can discover and connect to it.

Actually, for Icarus specifically, the community expects both 17777/UDP and 27015/UDP forwarded, but I'm noticing the Steam login itself failed in the logs (empty ID, no player found), which suggests the container lacks proper Steam credentials or a GSLT token—this could mean the SteamNetDriver never becomes functional regardless of port forwarding, making the whole port question potentially moot until authentication is resolved.

Actually, whether SteamNetDriver's port flag maps to a virtual Steam port versus a real socket is image/config territory that's out of scope — same class of owner decision as the Stationeers case. I'll document it as such and move on rather than trying to force a fix.

Let me just let the current job finish failing (a couple more attempts, roughly 20 minutes) and use that waiting time to write up progress notes instead.

Check Soulmask on a port it exposes, and stop counting loopback as bound

With Soulmask's setup script fixed (540d0a8) the server finally installs and
runs — and then still failed provisioning, on its health-check port.

`GAME_PORT.soulmask` was 18888/tcp, its echo/admin port. Read off the running
server's own namespace, that port is `0100007F:49C8` — 127.0.0.1:18888. It is
bound to loopback INSIDE the container, so `-p 18888:18888/tcp` publishes
nothing usable: docker-proxy accepts the connection and its dial to the backend
is refused, and an external connect gets "Connection refused" every time. The
ports actually on 0.0.0.0 are udp 8777 (game) and udp 27015 (query). Same shape
as Unturned's dead TCP publish, so the same resolution: the check port is now
the join port itself, and the join-port override it no longer needs is gone.

Moving a check from TCP to UDP used to weaken it. It does not any more —
bfbfdf1/7de3249 made a UDP pass require the socket to exist in the guest.

Which exposed the second half of this: `procNetHasPort` matched on port number
alone, so it would have called 127.0.0.1:18888 "bound" and cheerfully agreed
with a port proven unreachable from anywhere. It now skips loopback-bound
sockets — 127.0.0.0/8, ::1, and IPv4-mapped loopback. A socket bound to
loopback inside a container is on a network nobody else is on.

+3 tests. One existing fixture used 127.0.0.1 incidentally and now uses a real
address, so it still tests the LISTEN-state rule it was written for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Fix Nightingale's dead TCP check port, and two disks too small to install into

Both found by provisioning for real on node-2, and both were fatal to 100% of

NIGHTINGALE — WRONG PROTOCOL. `GAME_PORT` was 7777/tcp because the image maps
7777 on both. The server binds only udp 7777; its one TCP listener is 8888, and
its own log names Unreal's UDP `IpNetDriver`. So the TCP publish was dead and
the check could never pass. Same shape as Unturned and Soulmask, same fix: the
check port is the join port, no override. A UDP check is real evidence now that
provisioning also requires the socket to exist in the guest.

NIGHTINGALE — DISK. Its advertised 20GB entry tier cannot hold the game. A
fresh server with no player data yet sat at 19G used of 19G usable — 100% full,
95M free (11G of that is the game in the bind mount, the rest base image and
docker layers). It reached "ready_for_players = true" and would have died on
its first world save. The install baseline is identical on every tier, so all
three move together: 20/25/30 -> 30/35/40 GB.

world freshly generated and nobody playing. 25 -> 35 GB. The 40GB and 70GB tiers
already have room and are untouched.

linked-VPS-tier floor is gone ("treat that as a signal to fix the CATALOG entry")
— these are the third and fourth plans with hard on-node evidence, after Project
Zomboid and TF2. Live GamePlan rows synced to match. FLAGGED FOR THE OWNER:
bigger disks at the same price move the cost basis on both families.

+1 test.

content.thinking:
I've confirmed FAST_BOOT=true uses a script that skips the app_update validate step entirely, meaning the game files are never downloaded — this mode assumes data is already installed and is meant for restarting an existing server. So KF2 actually has two fatal issues: the config directory was never made writable, causing the crash loop, and FAST_BOOT skips installation entirely, so even fixing permissions wouldn't get the game files onto disk.

The fix requires both chmod-ing the directories and removing FAST_BOOT (or setting it false), which means SteamCMD will validate on every start — slower but correct, matching how most other catalog families handle updates. I'm weighing whether to test this by hand versus just fixing the seed/live row and re-provisioning, since the latter also tests whether the ~15-20GB KF2 install actually fits on the 19GB disk with only 13GB free, which looks borderline too small.

Given the entrypoint script already shows conclusive evidence, I'll skip the manual test and just apply the fix directly — editing the wave8 seed since that's where kf2 lives, then tearing down and re-provisioning to get the real verdict on both the fix and the disk size question.

cd /opt/nxeon && git add prisma/seed-wave8-games.ts && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Fix Killing Floor 2: one mount unwritable, and it never downloaded the game

Provisioned for real on node-2. Two independent faults, either fatal alone.

1. ONE OF TWO MOUNTS UNWRITABLE. The script chmod'd /opt/kf2/data but never
   /opt/kf2/config. The image checks both and refuses to start on either —
   "❌ Error: /config is not writeable!" — so the container exited immediately
   and systemd restarted it forever: caught at NRestarts=66 with 4.0K in each
   mount. Exactly the Left 4 Dead 2 shape from b97d143, which was also "one of
   its two mounts", and which this script's own half-chmod suggests nobody had
   run either.

2. FAST_BOOT SKIPPED THE INSTALL. Read out of the image's entrypoint:
   FAST_BOOT=true selects `steam-game-fast.script`, which lists the app id with
   no `app_update … validate` line at all, so SteamCMD downloads nothing. It is
   meant for restarting a server whose data volume is already populated. On a
   fresh order there is nothing to start — with the permissions fixed by hand
   the container got exactly that far and died on
   `./Binaries/Win64/KFGameSteamServer.bin.x86_64: No such file or directory`,
   with 8.0K in /data. Dropping the flag uses `steam-game.script`, which
   installs and validates. Same shape as the Garry's Mod fix (b6cf476), where
   the appid was never passed and SteamCMD also silently downloaded nothing.

Live OsTemplate row synced to match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

could not take a mod, and silently discarded anything edited into those
directories over SFTP or from the panel. Same class as the Left 4 Dead 2
(b97d143) and TF2/Squad/Mordhau (0eadce7) fixes. Note the uid is 1001 here,
